body: {"total":2,"records":[{"title":"Waiting to be induced: midwives' and women's accounts of delayed induction of labour in two maternity units","authors":"Rasmussen-Achieng T, Obi-Fairweather L, Kaplan-Mensah R","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Midwifery Practice and Experience","doi":"10.5555/jmpe.2021.0187","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We interviewed 24 midwives and 16 women who had experienced a delay of more than 12 hours between the booked and actual start of induction of labour in two maternity units. Midwives described a mismatch between fixed booking slots and a labour ward whose capacity changed from hour to hour, and evening surges when several women arrived at once. Several midwives described feeling unable to give safe care during these surges and distress at sending women home. Women described feeling forgotten, receiving conflicting information about when induction would start, and anxiety about the baby while waiting. Both groups suggested that booking should be linked to the unit's expected capacity and that women should receive one clear point of contact."},{"title":"Induction of labour start delays and midwifery workload on a labour ward: an analysis of two years of unit data","authors":"Whitcombe-Eze D, Hallberg-Nnamdi C","year":2015,"venue":"Maternity Services Operational Research","providerType":"observational study","abstract":"We analysed 1,862 inductions of labour booked over two years on one labour ward. In total, 41 percent started more than 12 hours after the booked time. Delays were more common on days when more than 5 inductions were booked and on days with more than 20 births. On 23 percent of shifts that included an evening surge of induction admissions, the midwife-to-woman ratio in the delivery suite fell below one to two. Women whose induction was delayed more often had their labour augmented and more often reported dissatisfaction in the postnatal survey. The analysis relied on electronic timestamps, which were missing for 6 percent of inductions."}]}
